title: Gideon and the Harbor
premise: Kestrel Kavanagh inherited a failing vineyard and a mountain of debt from a father who never said anything kind in his life. When a letter postmarked eleven years ago falls out of a wall during renovation—a letter from Marisol Reyes, the harbor-town sweetheart who vanished after one devastating summer—Kestrel learns the disappearance wasn't a choice but a coercion orchestrated by Kestrel's own father to protect a business deal. Chasing the truth to the harbor, Kestrel finds Marisol running the town's beloved festival, still guarded, still furious, and still impossible to forget. As debts, a predatory developer, and a decade of silence close in, Kestrel must choose between selling the vineyard to escape ruin and staying to rebuild both the land and a love they once let slip away—ending with the festival's last night, when Kestrel asks Marisol to stay after the final train leaves, and she does.
about_author: Dominic Lockridge is a former dockworker's son who spent a decade writing shipping manifests before turning to love stories set in working coastal towns. He lives above a shuttered cannery, where he collects unsent letters and insists they always find their way home.

chapters.title: The Weight of Dry Soil
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel audits the vineyard's ruin: foreclosed equipment, a father's debts, a bank letter with a thirty-day deadline. A developer's card sits on the kitchen table like a loaded gun. The emotional beat is exhausted resignation—the belief that second chances are for people with better timing.

chapters.title: What the Wall Kept
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Tearing out water-damaged plaster in the old farmhouse, Kestrel finds a tin box: a letter postmarked eleven years ago, from Marisol Reyes, begging Kestrel to meet her the night before she vanished. The beat is vertigo—everything Kestrel believed about being abandoned cracks open.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Weather
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, with a flashback to the last summer. Kestrel rereads the letter a dozen times, memory contradicting memory: the harbor, the bonfire, Marisol's empty seat on the last train. The beat is grief rekindled into something sharper—questions that won't stay buried.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed Nothing
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel confronts the family lawyer, who lets slip that Kestrel's father handled 'the Reyes situation' personally before he died. The beat is cold dread—the first hint that the disappearance wasn't Marisol's choice, and that the family name is stained.

chapters.title: Down to the Harbor
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel drives to the coastal town, telling themselves it's about the letter, not the person. The harbor has gentrified at the edges but the festival grounds remain. The beat is nervous hope curdling into fear at the sight of Marisol's name on the festival banner.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Runs the Tide
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. We meet Marisol mid-festival-planning, competent and armored, beloved by the town she adopted after fleeing her own. She sees Kestrel across the pier and the beat is fury—eleven years of hurt arriving in one unwelcome face.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Cannery Door
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Marisol refuses to hear Kestrel out; Kestrel refuses to leave without answers. Their argument draws a crowd, and Marisol's found-family—the festival volunteers—close ranks around her. The beat is public humiliation and private devastation for them both.

chapters.title: The Letter She Never Sent
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Alone, Marisol rereads her own draft replies to a letter she never mailed, revealing she wrote to Kestrel for years before giving up. The beat is aching tenderness under the armor—she never stopped, she only stopped hoping.

chapters.title: Terms of Truce
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A town elder forces them into proximity: the festival needs a wine vendor, and Kestrel's vineyard needs exposure. They agree to a business-only arrangement. The beat is wary détente—two people negotiating peace terms with their hearts off the table, or so they claim.

chapters.title: Old Ghosts, New Debts
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The developer, Vance Corliss, appears in the harbor town—he wants the festival grounds too, and he's been courting the bank holding Kestrel's loans. The beat is rising threat: the past and the present are converging on the same villain.

chapters.title: What Her Father Knew
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finally reveals her side: eleven years ago, Kestrel's father threatened her family's fishing licenses and her father's freedom unless she left town and never contacted Kestrel again. The beat is betrayal detonating—Kestrel's inheritance includes the weapon used against her.

chapters.title: The Vineyard Between Them
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel returns home to find Corliss's offer upgraded and the bank's deadline moved up. Tending the dead vines at night, Kestrel realizes the land was never the inheritance—the silence was. The beat is moral reckoning: what is Kestrel willing to give up to make this right?

chapters.title: Harvest Hands
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Kestrel returns to the harbor uninvited and offers to fund the festival from the last of the vineyard's reserves—an apology in action, not words. Marisol accepts the money but not the apology. The beat is grudging respect taking root where love used to be.

chapters.title: The Volunteers' Table
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol's found family—Rosa the fisherwoman, Dev the sound tech, old Tomas—debate whether Kestrel deserves a chance, forcing Marisol to admit she's still deciding herself. The beat is warmth and friction: found family as both shelter and mirror.

chapters.title: Corliss Makes His Move
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Corliss leverages Kestrel's debt to pressure the town council, offering to save the vineyard only if Kestrel withdraws from the festival and testifies the harbor grounds are blighted. The beat is the trap closing: love against duty, priced in acreage.

chapters.title: The Midnight Cellar
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Kestrel and Marisol, working late in the festival cellar, finally speak honestly—about the letter, the coercion, the years. A near-kiss is interrupted by a council summons. The beat is aching intimacy interrupted, desire and duty colliding mid-breath.

chapters.title: Council of Ashes
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At the council meeting, Kestrel publicly refuses Corliss, sacrificing the vineyard's rescue to defend the festival grounds. Marisol witnesses it. The beat is costly integrity—Kestrel loses the land's future and gains something harder: the right to be believed.

chapters.title: What We Bury, What We Plant
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Marisol shows Kestrel her father's hidden evidence—documents proving Kestrel's father's coercion, enough to void Corliss's claims. Together they plan to expose everything at the festival. The beat is alliance becoming partnership becoming something neither will name yet.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Festival
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Preparations spiral; Corliss files an injunction; Marisol wavers, terrified of losing the town she built. Kestrel stays without being asked, fixing what breaks. The beat is quiet devotion—the slow, unglamorous proof that staying is a language.

chapters.title: Festival of Reckoning
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the festival's peak, the evidence is read aloud before the town; Corliss's deal collapses as the community rallies. The beat is cathartic triumph—power's corruption exposed in the open air, and a town choosing its people over its price.

chapters.title: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. With the festival ending and the vineyard's fate still uncertain, Kestrel stands at the platform where it all began and asks Marisol to stay after the last train leaves—not for the town, not for the past, but for them. The beat is raw, trembling hope.

chapters.title: After the Whistle Fades
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The last train departs empty-handed of them both. On the vineyard's first replanted hillside, Kestrel and Marisol toast with the vineyard's first new pressing; the town's lights glitter below like a found family keeping watch. The beat is earned homecoming—love chosen over duty, and duty transformed by love.
